# VVC Is Versatile Enough for Streaming Needs


Learn how Versatile Video Coding (VVC) improves compression efficiency, reduces bitrate and supports high-quality streaming across 4K, 8K, VR and more.


September 2026


[VVC](https://www.interdigital.com/blog?tags=VVC)[Video](https://www.interdigital.com/blog?tags=Video)[Video Codecs](https://www.interdigital.com/blog?tags=Video%20Codecs)


As global demand for video continues to grow, it is critical to adapt to and enhance the ways audiences enjoy content. As a leader in wireless, video, and AI research, InterDigital continues to advance video compression techniques to meet the demand of the moment.


Compression is critical to achieving a balance between bitrate efficiency and visual quality as video makes its way through production, encoding, delivery, decoding, rendering, and display at the end user device. InterDigital has been innovating and contributing to the Versatile Video Coding (VVC) standard to enhance, simplify, and personalize the delivery of premium video content to all audiences.


## **What is VVC?**


Finalized in 2020 by the Joint Video Experts Team (JVET), VVC is a state-of-the-art codec that consistently performs at a[high level of visual fidelity](https://signalprocessingsociety.org/sites/default/files/uploads/community_involvement/docs/ICME2020_MMSPTC_VideoSlides_Versatile_Video_Coding.pdf) compared to previous codecs. VVC is an evolution from High Efficiency Video Coding (HEVC), or H.265. VVC offers enhanced features, including 65 intra directions (compared to HEVC’s 33), rectangular blocks for partitioning (while HEVC primarily uses squares), and 128x128 root blocks (HEVC’s blocks are 64x64). In sum, VVC’s versatility of compression options makes it more efficient than HEVC, while maintaining premium image quality.


When video is compressed, it is split into smaller and smaller blocks in a process that is called block partitioning. The most common split in block partitioning is the Quad Tree (QT) split, where video is split into four squares of equal proportion. HEVC primarily uses QT splits to compress video, but VVC refines this process, first dividing blocks using the QT split, and then allowing more freedom and versatility for the second split to allow for rectangular splits that achieve higher image detail and quality compared to HEVC. VVC’s two-stage splitting method delivers a higher focus than HEVC, essentially dividing the work in half while maintaining quality.


This evolution allows VVC to deliver significant bitrate reduction compared to HEVC. For typical smartphone users regularly streaming HD content at 3GB per hour, the use of VVC could translate to a[decrease in data usage of 900 megabytes per hour and 2.2 terabytes per year](https://greyb.com/blog/can-better-video-codecs-save-the-environment/) , resulting in lower energy consumption and decreased emissions in the network.


VVC could also help with cost reduction for cloud storage platforms by enabling them to host higher volumes of video content at a lower data cost. For streaming companies and broadcasters, VVC offers the same benefits, and the codec’s 30-50% bitrate reduction would allow streaming companies to offer premium quality content at lower cost or higher margins.


## “V” is for Versatility


Bitrate efficiency is among VVC’s strengths, but its standout characteristic is its application versatility. HEVC was designed to serve the demand for 4K, but the “versatile” in VVC makes it compatible with a wide range of video formats, from low-resolution to ultra-high-definition video formats like 4K, 8K, and even VR/360 **°** immersive video.


Intentionally designed to support different applications from the ground up, VVC distinguishes itself from previous codecs that began slowly accommodating new applications of video, by delivering 2D video over smartphones as easily as immersive content on a VR headset.


Reference Picture Resampling is another example of VVC’s versatility, because it enables the codec to use previously decoded pictures as references, even when their resolution differs from the current picture. This supports seamless changes in video size without interrupting the bitstream or restarting the coding sequence. This native flexibility is especially valuable for adaptive streaming and mobile video, where network and device conditions can change at any moment, representing a clear advantage over HEVC and earlier-generation codecs.


## Industry Interest


In recent years, Brazil and China have been among VVC’s strongest proponents. In 2025, the Brazilian government[made VVC an official and integral component](https://forumsbtvd.org.br/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/SBTVD-TV_3_0-P3-VC-Report.pdf) of its revamped TV broadcasting system, DTV+ or TV 3.0, whose commercial launch coincided with the start of the 2026 FIFA World Cup. In China, some of the country’s largest tech companies, Tencent, ByteDance, and[Huawei](https://www.mc-if.org/blog/mc-if-welcomes-huawei-and-looks-forward-to-growing-vvc-deployment/) have begun actively exploring VVC adoption, and in the Taiwan region, MediaTek’s Dimensity 9600 Pro is the[first smartphone processor](https://www.mediatek.com/products/smartphones/mediatek-dimensity-9600-pro) to include VVC hardware decode support for streaming video. In the U.S., VVC implementation has been slow, but interest is gradually growing – as signified by VVC’s full specifications published within ATSC 3.0 this April, and expanded codec support from companies like[Intel](https://www.sportsvideo.org/2025/02/07/vvc-gains-momentum-in-2024-adoption-milestones-set-stage-for-breakthroughs-in-2025/) and[Google](https://techcrunch.com/2026/02/11/google-releases-the-first-beta-of-android-17-adopts-a-continous-developer-release-plan/) .


Amidst growing interest in key regions, the biggest obstacle to VVC implementation is support from existing electronics hardware. System-on-Chips (SoCs) supporting VVC are available for TV sets and set-top boxes (STBs), and the launch of DTV+ in Brazil offers an incentive to bring VVC-compatible TVs and STBs to the market.


Video codecs like VVC define decoding methods, but do not define the encoder. Standards typically define the output structure for encoders, but require decoders to conform to the toolkit, which supports greater interoperability across a range of applications. On smartphones, tablets, and other mobile devices, VVC can be implemented using software decoders, but the ecosystem will increasingly depend on hardware decoders to unlock VVC’s full potential.


## What’s Next


Innovation around VVC continues, and at IBC 2026, InterDigital and NHK (Japan Broadcasting Corporation) were recognized for their demonstration of VVC Multilayer Coding, which enables multiple versions of video content to be carried within a coordinated VVC bitstream. This joint InterDigital - NHK demo was awarded “[Best in Show](https://www.interdigital.com/post/interdigital-and-nhk-awarded-ibc-best-in-show-for-vvc-multilayer-coding) ” for showing two aspects of the VVC Multilayer Main 10 profile that enables broadcasters and streamers to more efficiently and flexibly deliver high-quality, personalized content, and promotes its wider adoption in real-world services.


VVC multilayer coding supports more efficient delivery of different or enhanced versions of the same content, bypassing the need to independently encode and distribute every resolution. Ultimately, VVC multilayer coding enables broadcasters and streaming providers to flexibly and efficiently serve multiple resolutions from a coordinated bitstream, offering greater efficiency than simulcast for broadcasters and saving storage in streaming applications.


InterDigital’s innovation underpins the delivery of premium video content across a variety of devices. As the streaming ecosystem evolves and audience needs diversify, we continue to innovate and contribute to enhancements to the VVC standard that facilitate more efficient delivery of premium content to audiences everywhere.
